title: Banks look to shore up AI defences
full_text:
Hackers Protection against digital crime is high on board agendas.
When the board of the Commonwealth Bank meets in a fortnight to sign off on its full-year results, cybersecurity will be right at the top of the agenda. There is no doubt that's where it will be when its major rivals call their own board meetings in coming weeks.
How the country's biggest financial institutions confront the threat that their systems will be compromised by criminals turbocharged with artificial intelligence is no longer a second tier problem. It is becoming the defining challenge of the year ahead.
Things are moving rapidly. The development of Mythos, Anthropic's powerful AI tool that has managed to quickly detect decades-old flaws in software, and the looming arrival of plenty of rival models that will be equally powerful, is pushing companies to shake up long-held defence plans.
For years, senior executives would typically be required to approve a response to an incident, taking down a compromised computer system before the problem spread. Sometimes, this could take a day. Executives were unavailable, or overseas. Lengthy deliberation was required.
Now banks are considering whether to push responsibility for these decisions way down the org chart, to staff closer to operations, given the risk that AI will wreak havoc far faster once it detects a vulnerability.
"Crisis response used to plan for the first 24 to 48 hours, but now we're down to the first hour," says Nicole Quinn, the vice president for policy and government affairs at San Francisco-based Palo Alto Networks.
"You can't afford to wait for all the board members to join a call, or for senior leaders to get on Zoom. You need a pre-agreed response plan, approved by the board and CEO, so security teams can just pull the trigger."
Palo Alto Networks is one of the world's largest cybersecurity companies and its Unit 42 division is advising some of Australia's major banks on how to shift their defences. In the past, a software vulnerability would be actively exploited in about nine days, Quinn says. Last year, Unit 42 started seeing exploits used within three hours. Now, it is down to 25 minutes.
Anthropic said in June that it would not publicly release Mythos, citing the cybersecurity risks given that the model is adept at identifying unknown flaws in defences, putting the entire global financial system at risk. That left banks and other major companies scrambling for access, hoping to plug holes in their networks and systems before it was released.
Mythos' capabilities are game-changing because it can chain multiple, lower-level vulnerabilities together to create new attack paths to break into bank systems. Those problems will only worsen as more powerful models, including open-source versions made by Chinese developers, are released.
Anthropic began its staggered launch of Mythos on April 7, when it provided access to about 50 Wall Street and technology firms under an initiative it dubbed Project Glasswing. The collaborative effort was aimed at using the model to identify and fix software vulnerabilities before a broader public release would put critical services and infrastructure at risk.
By May 22, those companies had found "more than 10,000 high- or critical-severity vulnerabilities across the most systemically important software".
Open-source Chinese AI models are expected to have cutting-edge hacking capability later this year, but Quinn says Anthropic's Mythos Preview is a highly capable hacker today. Palo Alto Networks is one of the members of Project Glasswing that was granted early access to the frontier model.
On average, the company used to find three or four vulnerabilities a month across its systems. When it ran Mythos in June, it found 26, covering 75 total issues. "Mythos picked up in weeks what would have taken our best penetration testing teams about 12 months [to find]," Quinn adds.
Other developers such as OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, are also releasing increasingly sophisticated tools that can go off-piste. Last week, an OpenAI-powered agent hacked into Hugging Face, an AI start-up that hosts models and datasets for developers, after escaping from a testing environment. The tool gained internet access and stole login credentials without direction. The increasing sophistication is pushing boards to move away from the checklist-based approach that has dominated cybersecurity governance for the past decade. Regulators are asking these companies to shift to risk-based guidelines that require a more in-depth understanding of where actual threats lie and how a hack can ripple across the whole bank.
This comes after the Australian Signals Directorate, a government agency that conducts cybersecurity operations, said last month it would retire guidelines known as the Essential Eight that it had recommended boards use for decades. The agency said the checklist-style guidelines had become too rigid to respond to the threat of autonomous agents powered by AI.
"We are moving to an approach which means boards need to engage more with what risks actually look like, and how [managers] are testing and proving controls are in place and effective," says Ross Phillipson, a cybersecurity partner at Gilbert+Tobin.
"They should not be asking about green checklists, or which bits are in orange - because a checklist doesn't give you insight. It's just a point-in-time assessment that doesn't have any direct linkage to what the risk is."
Despite the new-found attention, advisers who work with global banks suggest Australia is nowhere near the forefront of cyberdefence preparedness, adding that many boards lack technology skills.
"Australia is in the middle of the pack on this," says Rico Brandenburg, a New York-based partner at Oliver Wyman, who runs the consulting firm's global cybersecurity practice.
"The rules [that the corporate and banking regulations] have put in place are a good starting point, to make sure cyber is at the top of executives' minds. "It's now up to institutions to use regulatory guidance and reduce exposures and accelerate strategic uplift."
The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority is already urging banks to think more carefully about the types of threats they will face.
Last month, the regulator's chairman, John Lonsdale, said that awareness of the threats had "not always been matched by practical action".
